followUps:
The filter runs during the first pass, before any frame is unwound, so the stack is still exactly as it was at the throw. That lets a debugger or a logging call see every local variable and the full call chain.

A normal catch only runs after unwinding, when inner frames and their finally blocks are already gone. Example: if Work() calls Parse() and Parse throws, a filter in Main still sees Parse and Work on the stack.

A first-chance exception is the notification that an exception has just been thrown, before the runtime knows whether anything will handle it. Debuggers can break on it, and AppDomain.FirstChanceException fires for it.

Most first-chance exceptions are caught later and are harmless, for example a parse that fails inside a library and is handled. A second-chance (unhandled) exception means no handler was found and the process is about to terminate. Many first-chance exceptions in a hot loop are a performance warning sign.

code.title: Handler search: filter first, finally second

followUps:
Not any more for ordinary custom exceptions: binary serialization of exceptions is obsolete, and in .NET 8 the protected serialization constructor is no longer needed. BinaryFormatter is disabled by default and flagged as unsafe.

Keep the three usual constructors (none, message, message plus inner exception) and your own data constructor. You only keep the SerializationInfo constructor if you must support old .NET Framework remoting or a library that still serializes exceptions with it.

Usually yes, seal it unless you really want others to derive from it. A sealed type is simpler to reason about, and callers catching it know exactly what they get.

Leave it unsealed only for a deliberate base type of a family, for example PaymentException with CardDeclinedException and InsufficientFundsException below it. Then callers can catch the base to handle the whole family, or a derived type for one case. Do not add depth just in case.

code.title: Custom exception carrying retry data

followUps:
It captures an exception together with its stack trace so you can rethrow it later, even on a different thread, without losing the original trace. Plain throw ex; would reset the trace to the rethrow line.

Example: a worker thread stores ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(e); the caller thread later calls edi.Throw();. The new trace shows the original frames, then a marker line such as 'End of stack trace from previous location', then the rethrow site. Task and await use this idea internally.

code.title: throw vs throw ex vs wrapping

followUps:
If the filter throws, the exception it throws is swallowed and the filter counts as returning false. The search then continues to the next catch clause as if the condition had not matched.

The original exception keeps flying and the filter's own exception is lost, so a bug inside a filter is silent. Example: when (Lookup(e.Message) == 1) where Lookup throws on null means this clause is skipped. Keep filters small and side-effect light, and wrap risky calls in their own try.

code.title: Filter that logs without unwinding

followUps:
await using calls DisposeAsync() and awaits it, instead of calling Dispose() synchronously. It is for types implementing IAsyncDisposable, such as ones that flush a buffer over the network.

await using (var w = new AsyncWriter())
{
    await w.WriteAsync("x");
}   // awaits w.DisposeAsync() here

The method must be async. The disposal order is still reverse acquisition, and a class can implement both interfaces.

The exception from Dispose replaces the one already in flight, so the original error is lost. That is a known trap, since the first exception is usually the real cause.

Example: the body throws A, finally runs Dispose, Dispose throws B, and the caller sees only B. So Dispose should avoid throwing: swallow or log cleanup errors, and never make Close or Dispose do work that commonly fails. Some APIs do this on purpose, for example by catching in their Dispose.

code.title: using disposes in reverse order

followUps:
Because by the time a finalizer runs, the garbage collector may already have finalized or reclaimed the other objects, and their finalization order is not defined. Touching them could use a dead or half-released object.

That is why Dispose(false) only frees your own unmanaged resource, such as one native handle, and skips managed fields. Those fields have their own finalizers if they need them. Example: a field holding a FileStream might already be finalized, so call its Dispose only when disposing is true.

code.title: Dispose pattern with SuppressFinalize

followUps:
They are attributes that teach the compiler's null analysis about what your method really does, so callers see fewer false warnings. They only affect warnings, not runtime behaviour.

[NotNullWhen(true)] on an out parameter says it is not null when the method returns true, so if (dict.TryGetValue(k, out var v)) v.Length is clean. [MemberNotNull(nameof(Name))] on a method says that after it runs the field is set, so a constructor calling Init() no longer warns about an uninitialised non-nullable field.

Migrate in small steps: turn the feature on per project or per file, fix warnings, then tighten. Trying to fix everything in one go is slow and risky.

  1. Add <Nullable>annotations</Nullable> or #nullable enable to leaf libraries first.
  2. Annotate public APIs, since callers depend on them.
  3. Switch to enable and fix the warnings.
  4. Finally treat nullable warnings as errors.

Avoid sprinkling !; it hides real bugs.

code.title: Nullable annotations do not enforce at runtime

followUps:
It tells the compiler the type argument must be a non-nullable type: a value type, or a reference type that is not marked nullable. Passing string? to where T : notnull produces a warning.

class Cache<TKey> where TKey : notnull
{
    Dictionary<TKey, int> map = new();
}

That matches Dictionary, which cannot use null as a key. It is checked at compile time only, and warns rather than errors.

code.title: Unconstrained T? and default values

followUps:
Lifted operators mean that comparisons with a null int? do not behave like ordinary numbers. null < 5, null > 5 and null == 5 are all false, and null != 5 is true.

So !(a < b) is not the same as a >= b when either is null. With a = null, b = 5: a < b is false, and a >= b is false too, so the two checks are both false. Also null + 1 is null. Check HasValue or use ?? before comparing.

code.title: Sentinel vs int? vs TryFind

followUps:
For a simple switch on integers or strings, the compiler picks a lookup strategy instead of testing arms one by one. With a few arms it emits an if chain, with a dense range of integers it emits a jump table, and with many string arms it computes a hash and jumps.

For patterns it builds a decision tree that never tests the same thing twice: if three arms check the same property, it reads it once. So order matters mostly for readability, apart from arms with guards, which run in order.

code.title: Switch statement features: goto case, guards

followUps:
Constant, relational and the parts of logical patterns built from them need compile-time constants. Type, var, discard, property, positional and list patterns do not need constants themselves.

Example: x is 5 and x is > 10 and < 20 are fine, but x is > limit fails if limit is a normal variable, since the right side must be a constant (const int limit = 5 works). When you need a runtime value, use a when guard: case int n when n > limit.

code.title: Pattern kinds via is and as

followUps:
You build a closed set of cases yourself, using either a sealed base class with private constructor and sealed nested types, or records plus a switch with a throwing discard arm.

abstract record Result;
sealed record Ok(int V) : Result;
sealed record Err(string Msg) : Result;
string Show(Result r) => r switch {
  Ok o => $"ok {o.V}", Err e => e.Msg,
  _ => throw new InvalidOperationException() };

The compiler cannot prove completeness without the discard arm, so add tests for each case.

code.title: Type switch over a closed set of shapes

followUps:
Both are special: the runtime usually cannot be trusted to continue after them, so you normally do not catch them. A StackOverflowException cannot be caught at all and ends the process immediately.

OutOfMemoryException can be caught, but memory may still be tight and state may be half-built, so the safe move is to fail fast, or, for a single large request that failed to allocate, reject that request. A broad catch (Exception) does catch OOM, which is another reason to keep it at the outermost boundary, where you log and shut down cleanly.

code.title: Narrow catches inside, broad catch at the boundary

followUps:
Create a benchmark class with one method that throws and catches, and one that uses TryXxx, and let the tool run them many times. Single Stopwatch timings are noisy because of JIT and warm-up, so a benchmark library is better.

[MemoryDiagnoser]
public class Bench {
  [Benchmark] public int Throw() { try { return int.Parse("x"); } catch { return -1; } }
  [Benchmark] public int TryIt() => int.TryParse("x", out var v) ? v : -1;
}

Run in Release mode. Expect the throwing version to be microseconds and allocate memory, while TryParse takes nanoseconds.

code.title: Exception path vs TryParse cost

followUps:
Because finally must always complete, and a return would silently cancel an exception or an earlier return that is already on its way. The compiler rejects it with error CS0157: control cannot leave the body of a finally clause.

Example: if the try body threw an exception and finally said return 0;, the exception would disappear without any trace. The same applies to break, continue and goto that jump out of the block. Use finally only for cleanup.
